intro: Te Araroa is a small town on New Zealand's East Cape, in the Gisborne region, reached by a long coastal drive from Gisborne. Beside the school stands Te Waha o Rerekohu, a pohutukawa that its own sign calls well over 350 years old and about 40 metres across. You can see it from Moana Parade along the beachfront, and looking costs nothing.

trees.story:
The sign beside this pohutukawa gives it a name, Te Waha o Rerekohu, the mouth of Rerekohu, and says the local school is named after it. Rerekohu was an ancestor of the people of this district. The sign sets out his line of descent and gives two accounts of how the tree got its name, one about a house that stood beside it and food brought as tribute to feed the child Rerekohu.

It puts the tree at well in excess of 350 years old and 40 metres across at its widest, and calls it reputed to be the largest of its species in the world. The New Zealand Herald describes it as nearly 40 metres wide and almost 20 metres high. The reader who sent the photograph puts it at 600 years, by their estimate, and tourist pages repeat that figure, but none we found says how it was reached, so the sign's figure stands.

The photograph shows why people stop. Thick limbs twist out from a short trunk and arch back toward the ground under a dark canopy, and the whole mass is far wider than it is tall. A notice asks visitors not to climb on it. The Herald has reported that myrtle rust was found on the tree.

It can be seen from Moana Parade along the beachfront at Te Araroa.
